stem: Which state of matter has a fixed volume but no fixed shape?

options.rationale: A solid has a fixed shape as well as a fixed volume.
A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container.
A gas has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume: it spreads out to fill its container.

options.content: Both a liquid and a gas
options.rationale: A gas does not have a fixed volume, so only the liquid fits the description.

explanation: The particles of a liquid stay close together, so its volume is fixed, but they can slide past one another, so a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.
hints: Think about pouring water from a jug into a glass: does its volume change? Does its shape?

stem: Which description fits the particles in a **solid**?

options.content: Close together in a regular arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions
options.rationale: Strong forces hold the particles of a solid in fixed positions, but they still vibrate.

options.content: Close together in a random arrangement, sliding past each other
options.rationale: This describes the particles in a liquid.

options.content: Far apart in a random arrangement, moving quickly in all directions
options.rationale: This describes the particles in a gas.

options.content: Close together in a regular arrangement, not moving at all
options.rationale: The particles in a solid are not still: they vibrate about fixed positions.

explanation: In a solid the particles are touching, arranged in a regular pattern (a lattice) and vibrate about fixed positions. The vibration gets stronger as the solid is heated.
hints: Remember the three things to describe: arrangement, separation and motion.

stem: Which change of state **gives out** energy to the surroundings?

options.rationale: Melting takes in energy so that the particles can break out of their fixed positions.
Boiling takes in energy so that the particles can overcome the forces between them and escape.
Evaporation takes in energy: the fastest particles escape from the surface, which is why sweating cools you.
As a gas condenses, its particles slow down and are pulled together by the forces of attraction, giving out energy.

explanation: Changes that pull particles closer together (condensation and freezing) give out energy. Changes that separate particles (melting, boiling and evaporation) take energy in, because the forces of attraction have to be overcome.
hints: Which change makes the particles move closer together?

stem: True or false: the particles in a solid do not move.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not quite: the particles in a solid **vibrate** about fixed positions. Only their positions are fixed.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: the particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions, and they vibrate more strongly when the solid is heated.

explanation: According to the kinetic particle theory, the particles of every substance are always moving. In a solid they cannot move from place to place, but they vibrate about fixed positions.
hints: What happens to the particles of a solid when it is heated, just before it melts?

stem: Substance P melts at $-39\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and boils at $357\ ^\circ\text{C}$. What is the state of P at $20\ ^\circ\text{C}$?

options.rationale: P is a solid only below its melting point of $-39\ ^\circ\text{C}$, and $20\ ^\circ\text{C}$ is warmer than that.
$20\ ^\circ\text{C}$ is above the melting point and below the boiling point.
P only becomes a gas above $357\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

options.content: A mixture of solid and liquid
options.rationale: Solid and liquid are present together only at the melting point itself, $-39\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

explanation: A substance is a liquid at any temperature between its melting point and its boiling point. $20\ ^\circ\text{C}$ lies between $-39\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and $357\ ^\circ\text{C}$, so P is a liquid.
hints: Is $20\ ^\circ\text{C}$ below the melting point, between the two values, or above the boiling point?

stem: Match each change of state with its description. One description is not used.

right.content: Liquid to gas from the surface, below the boiling point
Liquid to gas throughout the liquid, at the boiling point

explanation: Melting is solid to liquid and freezing is the reverse. Condensation is gas to liquid. Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid below its boiling point; the unused description is boiling, which happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point.

stem: **Supplement.** Complete the explanation of melting.

payload.template: When a solid is heated, its particles gain {{blank:energy}} energy and vibrate more strongly. At the {{blank:point}} point they have enough energy to overcome some of the forces of {{blank:forces}} that hold them in fixed positions, so they begin to slide past each other.

explanation: Heating gives the particles more kinetic energy. At the melting point they can overcome some of the forces of attraction holding them in the regular arrangement, so the solid becomes a liquid.
hints: The energy of moving particles is called kinetic energy.

stem: Why can a gas be compressed much more easily than a liquid?

options.content: Gas particles are far apart, with large empty spaces between them.
options.rationale: Compressing a gas only pushes its particles into some of the empty space between them.

options.content: Gas particles are smaller than liquid particles.
options.rationale: The particles of a substance are the same size in every state; only their separation changes.

options.content: Gas particles move more slowly than liquid particles.
options.rationale: Gas particles do not move more slowly, and speed is not what makes a gas easy to compress: the large spaces between its particles are.

options.content: Gas particles can be squashed into smaller particles.
options.rationale: Particles are not squashed when a gas is compressed: the spaces between them become smaller.

explanation: The particles of a liquid are already touching, so they cannot be pushed much closer together. In a gas there are large spaces between the particles, so pressure can push them closer together and the volume decreases.
hints: Compare how close together the particles are in a liquid and in a gas.

stem: Which statement is true for evaporation but **not** for boiling?

options.content: It takes place only at the surface of the liquid.
options.rationale: Boiling happens throughout the liquid, with bubbles of gas forming inside it.

options.content: The liquid takes in energy from its surroundings.
options.rationale: Both evaporation and boiling take in energy.

options.content: Particles escape from the liquid and become a gas.
options.rationale: In both processes particles escape and form a gas.

options.content: For a pure liquid, it happens at one fixed temperature.
options.rationale: This is true of boiling: a pure liquid boils at its boiling point. Evaporation happens over a range of temperatures.

explanation: Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid at temperatures below the boiling point, when the fastest particles escape. Boiling happens at the boiling point, throughout the liquid. Both turn liquid into gas and both take in energy.
hints: Think about where the particles escape from in each process.

stem: Rudo leaves a saucer of water on a windowsill in Gweru. Two days later the saucer is dry, although the water never boiled. Name the process by which the water left the saucer.

rejected.feedback: The water never reached its boiling point. Escape of particles from the surface below the boiling point is evaporation.
Condensation is gas turning into liquid, the reverse of what happened here.

explanation: The fastest-moving water particles at the surface escaped into the air, little by little, at room temperature. This is evaporation.
hints: Which change of state happens at the surface of a liquid below its boiling point?

stem: **Supplement.** A balloon full of air is carried from a cool room into hot sunshine. The air pressure outside stays the same, but the balloon becomes bigger. Which statement explains this?

options.content: The air particles move faster and hit the inside of the balloon harder and more often, so the gas expands.
options.rationale: Faster particles push outwards more, and the stretchy balloon lets the gas expand until the pressures balance again.

options.content: Each air particle gets bigger when it is heated.
options.rationale: Particles do not change size; the spaces between them increase.

options.content: Heating makes extra air particles inside the balloon.
options.rationale: The balloon is sealed: the number of particles stays the same.

options.content: The forces of attraction between the air particles become stronger.
options.rationale: The forces between gas particles are very weak, and stronger attractions would pull the particles together, not apart.

explanation: Heating gives the gas particles more kinetic energy. They collide with the walls of the balloon harder and more often, so the gas pushes outwards and expands until its pressure again matches the pressure outside.
hints: What happens to the speed of gas particles when the gas is heated?

stem: Select **all** the statements that are true for the particles in a **liquid**.

options.rationale: Liquid particles are close together and mostly touching.
There is no regular pattern in a liquid.

options.content: They can slide past each other.
options.rationale: This is why liquids flow.

options.content: They only vibrate about fixed positions.
options.rationale: This describes a solid.

options.content: They are far apart, with large spaces between them.
options.rationale: This describes a gas.

options.content: There are no forces of attraction between them.
options.rationale: The forces between liquid particles are weaker than in a solid but still significant: they keep the particles close together.

explanation: Liquid particles are close together (so a liquid has a fixed volume), randomly arranged and free to slide past one another (so a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container).
hints: A liquid has a fixed volume but can flow. Which statements explain both?

stem: The end of a syringe containing air is sealed. The plunger is slowly pushed in while the temperature stays the same. What happens?

options.content: The volume of the air decreases and its particles become smaller.
options.rationale: The particles do not shrink; only the spaces between them get smaller.

options.content: The volume stays the same and the particles move faster.
options.rationale: The volume does decrease, and at constant temperature the particles do not speed up.

options.content: The volume decreases because the air turns into a liquid.
options.rationale: Gently pushing a syringe at room temperature does not liquefy air; the gas is simply compressed.

options.content: The volume of the air decreases and its particles are closer together.
options.rationale: Increasing the pressure at constant temperature reduces the volume by reducing the spaces between particles.

explanation: At constant temperature, increasing the pressure on a gas decreases its volume. The same number of particles is pushed into a smaller space, so the particles are closer together and collide with the walls more often.
hints: Gases can be compressed because of the spaces between their particles.

stem:
A particle diagram shows a substance **before** and **after** a change.

- Before: the particles are far apart and moving quickly in all directions.
- After: the particles are touching, randomly arranged and sliding past each other.

Which change of state has taken place?

options.rationale: Boiling turns a liquid (particles touching) into a gas (particles far apart): the opposite direction.
The substance has changed from a gas to a liquid.
After freezing the particles would be in a regular arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions.
Melting starts with a solid, whose particles are in a regular arrangement.

explanation: Particles that are far apart and moving quickly in all directions are a gas; particles that are touching, random and sliding past each other are a liquid. Gas to liquid is condensation.
hints: Identify the state before and the state after first.

stem:
The table gives the melting points and boiling points of four substances, Q, R, S and T.

| Substance | Melting point / °C | Boiling point / °C |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Q | −182 | −162 |
| R | 17 | 118 |
| S | −117 | 78 |
| T | 801 | 1465 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which substance is a gas at $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$? Give its letter.
parts.explanation: Q boils at $-162\ ^\circ\text{C}$, so at $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$ it is well above its boiling point and is a gas.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which substance is a solid on a cold morning at $10\ ^\circ\text{C}$ but a liquid on a hot afternoon at $30\ ^\circ\text{C}$? Give its letter.
parts.explanation: R melts at $17\ ^\circ\text{C}$: below that it is solid and above it (up to $118\ ^\circ\text{C}$) it is liquid.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: What is the state of S at $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$?

options.rationale: S melts at $-117\ ^\circ\text{C}$, far below $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$.
S boils at $78\ ^\circ\text{C}$, so at $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$ it is no longer a liquid.
$100\ ^\circ\text{C}$ is above the boiling point of S.
Solid and liquid coexist only at the melting point.

parts.explanation: $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$ is above the boiling point of S ($78\ ^\circ\text{C}$), so S is a gas.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Which substance is a liquid over the widest range of temperature? Give its letter.
parts.explanation: The liquid ranges are Q: $20\ ^\circ\text{C}$, R: $101\ ^\circ\text{C}$, S: $195\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and T: $664\ ^\circ\text{C}$, so T has the widest range.

explanation: Compare each temperature with the melting and boiling points: below the melting point a substance is solid, between the two it is liquid, and above the boiling point it is gas. The liquid range is the boiling point minus the melting point.
workedSolution:
**(a)** Only Q has a boiling point below $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$, so Q is a gas.

**(b)** R melts at $17\ ^\circ\text{C}$, which lies between $10\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and $30\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

**(c)** S boils at $78\ ^\circ\text{C}$, so at $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$ it is a gas.

**(d)** Liquid ranges: Q $-162 - (-182) = 20$; R $118 - 17 = 101$; S $78 - (-117) = 195$; T $1465 - 801 = 664$. T is liquid over the widest range.
hints: Below the melting point: solid. Between the melting and boiling points: liquid. Above the boiling point: gas.
For (d), subtract the melting point from the boiling point for each substance. Take care with the negative values.

stem: Water exists as ice, liquid water and steam. This question is about the particles in each state.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: In which state do the particles only vibrate about fixed positions?

options.rationale: Liquid particles slide past each other.
Gas particles move quickly in all directions.
Ice is the solid: its particles are held in fixed positions.
In both of these states the particles move from place to place.

parts.explanation: In a solid the particles vibrate about fixed positions.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why steam can be compressed but liquid water cannot.

points.description: The particles in steam are far apart, with large spaces between them, so they can be pushed closer together
The particles in liquid water are already close together (touching), so they cannot be pushed much closer

parts.explanation: Compression reduces the spaces between particles. Steam has large spaces; liquid water has almost none.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: **Supplement.** Describe and explain what happens to the water particles when liquid water boils.

points.description: The particles gain (kinetic) energy from heating and move faster
At the boiling point they have enough energy to overcome the forces of attraction between them
They move far apart as a gas, escaping from throughout the liquid (bubbles form)

parts.explanation: Boiling separates the particles completely, which needs enough energy to overcome the attractions between them.

explanation: Ice particles vibrate about fixed positions. Steam is compressible because of the large spaces between its particles, whereas liquid water particles are already touching. On boiling, the particles gain enough energy to overcome the forces of attraction and move far apart as a gas.
workedSolution:
**(a)** Ice.

**(b)** Steam particles are far apart, so pressure can push them closer together; water particles are already touching, so the liquid hardly compresses.

**(c)** Heating gives the particles more kinetic energy, so they move faster. At $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$ (the boiling point) they have enough energy to overcome the forces of attraction between them, so they escape from all through the liquid as bubbles of gas and move far apart.
hints: Compression depends on the spaces between particles.
For boiling, mention energy and the forces between the particles.

stem: **Supplement.** A gas syringe contains some air. Its nozzle is sealed and its plunger can move freely, so the pressure of the air inside always equals the air pressure outside. The syringe is placed in a beaker of water, which is heated slowly from $20\ ^\circ\text{C}$ to $60\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What happens to the volume of the air in the syringe?

options.rationale: Cooling, not heating, makes the volume decrease at constant pressure.
The plunger is free to move, so the gas can expand.
The air keeps expanding as long as its temperature rises.
A gas expands when it is heated at constant pressure.

parts.explanation: At constant pressure the volume of a gas increases with temperature.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain your answer to (a) in terms of the air particles.

points.description: The particles gain kinetic energy and move faster
They collide with the walls of the syringe / the plunger harder and more often
So the plunger is pushed out and the gas expands until its pressure again equals the pressure outside

parts.explanation: Faster particles push harder on the plunger, so it moves out until the pressures balance.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The syringe is cooled back to $20\ ^\circ\text{C}$. The plunger is then pushed in and held, so that the air occupies a smaller volume at $20\ ^\circ\text{C}$. How has the pressure of the air changed?

options.rationale: A smaller volume at the same temperature means a higher pressure, not a lower one.
Squashing the gas into a smaller space changes the pressure.
The air still has particles colliding with the walls, so it still has a pressure.
The same number of particles in a smaller volume hit the walls more often.

parts.explanation: At constant temperature, decreasing the volume of a gas increases its pressure.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain, in terms of particles, your answer to (c).

points.description: The same number of particles is in a smaller space, so they collide with the walls more often (more collisions per second)

parts.explanation: The particles move at the same speed, but there are more of them in each cubic centimetre, so collisions with the walls are more frequent.

explanation: Heating at constant pressure makes gas particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often, so the gas expands. Compressing a gas at constant temperature packs the same particles into a smaller space, so they hit the walls more often and the pressure rises.
workedSolution:
**(a)** The volume increases.

**(b)** The particles gain kinetic energy and move faster; they hit the plunger harder and more often; the plunger moves out until the pressure inside equals the pressure outside, so the volume is larger.

**(c)** The pressure increases.

**(d)** The same number of particles is now in a smaller volume, so there are more collisions with the walls each second.
hints: Think about the speed of the particles in (a) and (b), and about how crowded they are in (c) and (d).

stem: True or false: when a liquid freezes, it gives out energy to its surroundings.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: as the particles are pulled into fixed positions by the forces of attraction, energy is given out.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Freezing gives energy out. That is why a liquid must be cooled (energy removed) for it to freeze.

explanation: Freezing is the reverse of melting. Melting takes in energy to overcome forces of attraction, so freezing gives out the same amount of energy as the particles are pulled into fixed positions.

stem:
**Supplement.** In many homes in rural Zimbabwe, drinking water is stored in an unglazed clay pot. A little water soaks through the clay and evaporates from the outside of the pot, and the water inside stays noticeably cooler than the air around it.

Use the kinetic particle theory to explain why the water in the pot stays cool. [5]

points.description: Water evaporates from the outer surface of the pot (below its boiling point)
The particles that escape are those with the most kinetic energy (the fastest-moving ones)
They have enough energy to overcome the forces of attraction of the surrounding particles
So the average kinetic energy of the particles left behind decreases
Lower average kinetic energy means a lower temperature: evaporation takes energy from the pot and the water inside it
Cooling is greater on a hot, dry or windy day because evaporation is faster

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Water that soaks through the clay **evaporates** from the outside of the pot. At any temperature some water particles move faster than others. Only the particles with the **most kinetic energy** can overcome the **forces of attraction** of their neighbours and escape into the air. Because the fastest particles leave, the **average kinetic energy** of the particles that remain falls, so their temperature falls. In this way evaporation takes energy from the pot and the water inside it, keeping the drinking water cool. The effect is greatest on hot, dry, windy days, when evaporation is fastest.
answerSpec.markingNotes: Award any five of the six points. Do not credit answers that say the water boils.

explanation: Evaporation removes the most energetic particles, so the average kinetic energy, and therefore the temperature, of the remaining water falls.
hints: Which particles are able to escape from the surface during evaporation?
Temperature is linked to the average kinetic energy of the particles.

stem: Substance X melts at $115\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and boils at $445\ ^\circ\text{C}$. Substance Y melts at $-7\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and boils at $59\ ^\circ\text{C}$. Both are heated from $20\ ^\circ\text{C}$ to $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$. Which statement is correct?

options.content: X melts; Y stays a liquid.
options.rationale: X does not reach its melting point of $115\ ^\circ\text{C}$, and Y boils at $59\ ^\circ\text{C}$.
Y is already a liquid at $20\ ^\circ\text{C}$, and X never reaches its melting point.

options.content: X stays a solid; Y changes from a liquid to a gas.
options.rationale: $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$ is below the melting point of X, and Y passes its boiling point of $59\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

options.content: X stays a solid; Y stays a liquid.
options.rationale: Y boils at $59\ ^\circ\text{C}$, which is below $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

explanation: At $20\ ^\circ\text{C}$ X is a solid (below $115\ ^\circ\text{C}$) and Y is a liquid (between $-7\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and $59\ ^\circ\text{C}$). At $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$ X is still a solid, but Y has passed its boiling point and is a gas.
hints: Work out the state of each substance at $20\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and again at $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$.
